title: Early Retirement Health Insurance Before Medicare at 65
metaDescription: Compare COBRA, Marketplace plans, and other early retirement health insurance options before 65. Learn the enrollment windows and questions to ask.
h1: Early Retirement Health Insurance Before Medicare
cardBlurb: Compare coverage choices before Medicare, including COBRA costs, Marketplace enrollment windows, and questions to ask before leaving your job.
introText:
If you retire before 65, your early retirement health insurance options include Marketplace plans, job-based continuation coverage, and any spouse's employer coverage available to you. At ModernWallet, we treat insurance costs as a line item to price before setting an early-retirement date.

[Medicare's](https://www.medicare.gov/basics/get-started-with-medicare/sign-up/when-does-medicare-coverage-start) Initial Enrollment Period begins three months before the month you turn 65. Coverage for the time before then takes its own plan. The price and enrollment deadline for each option deserve attention before you choose a date to leave your job.

sections.heading: The Coverage Gap Before Medicare
sections.body:
Retiring before 65 means you need to identify coverage for the time before Medicare enrollment approaches. Start with the coverage available through your job. Ask when it would end if you retired, since that date affects which enrollment windows you need to track.

The broad choices are continuation of a group plan under the [Consolidated Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act (COBRA)](https://www.dol.gov/agencies/ebsa/laws-and-regulations/laws/cobra), a Marketplace plan, and any coverage available through a spouse's employer. Other coverage options may exist for your situation. Ask a licensed insurance agent about options you cannot confirm through your employer or the Marketplace.

Put a possible retirement date beside the date your job-based coverage would end. Then ask for the cost and enrollment deadline of each available option. If one source of coverage would end before you reach Medicare eligibility, you need an answer for the remaining time as well. The [early retirement calculator](/retirement/early-retirement-calculator/) can help you place a quoted insurance cost alongside other retirement expenses.

sections.heading: COBRA for Early Retirement Health Insurance
sections.body:
COBRA can temporarily continue group health coverage for workers and families who lose job-based health benefits. It applies to employers with 20 or more employees. Ask your plan administrator whether COBRA would be available to you and any dependents when your job-based coverage ends.

COBRA coverage usually lasts up to 18 months. That may be shorter than the time between an early retirement date and Medicare eligibility, so compare the expected end of COBRA with your remaining coverage needs. Do not treat the usual duration as a promise that it will cover your whole gap.

You have 60 days to elect COBRA. The period starts when job-based coverage ends or when you receive the COBRA election notice, whichever is later. Keep both dates so you can identify the applicable deadline. Your plan administrator can confirm the notice date and explain the election materials for your plan.

You usually pay the full premium unless your employer agrees to cover some or all of it as part of your separation. The amount charged can be up to 102% of the plan's cost, according to the [U.S. Department of Labor's COBRA overview](https://www.dol.gov/general/topic/health-plans/cobra). Ask for the premium you would pay before comparing COBRA with a Marketplace quote.

sections.heading: Marketplace Coverage and the Special Enrollment Period
sections.body:
Losing qualifying health coverage may give you a Marketplace Special Enrollment Period. [HealthCare.gov](https://www.healthcare.gov/coverage-outside-open-enrollment/special-enrollment-period/) says you may qualify if you lost qualifying coverage in the past 60 days or expect to lose it in the next 60 days. Retirement itself is not listed there as a qualifying life event. Confirm how the loss of your job-based coverage applies before relying on a particular enrollment date.

COBRA decisions have their own timing consequences. Voluntarily dropping COBRA does not qualify you for a Special Enrollment Period, and choosing to stop paying COBRA premiums does not qualify either. When COBRA ends, HealthCare.gov lists a 60-day window. If you are comparing COBRA with Marketplace coverage, check the enrollment timing as well as the monthly price.

Premium tax credits depend on estimated household income. A Marketplace quote based on one income estimate may therefore be different from a quote based on another. Confirm current credit eligibility and plan prices with HealthCare.gov rather than assuming a credit will apply.

Taxable income planning can matter when you estimate income for coverage during early retirement. If a [Roth conversion ladder](/guides/roth-conversion-ladder/) is part of your broader research, ask a certified public accountant how a proposed conversion might affect the income estimate you provide. That conversation is separate from confirming Marketplace eligibility with HealthCare.gov.

sections.heading: Comparing Early Retirement Health Insurance Options
sections.body:
Compare COBRA and Marketplace coverage using quotes and dates for the coverage you could use. The COBRA premium comes from the group plan's administrator. A Marketplace price needs to be checked using your estimated household income, since premium tax credits depend on that estimate. If coverage through a spouse's employer is an option, ask that plan administrator for its price and enrollment rules.

Cost is only one comparison. Ask each plan for its provider information if you want to know whether particular clinicians are included. Check the coverage dates against your expected retirement date and the start of any replacement coverage. A lower quoted premium does not answer either of those questions.

COBRA may suit someone who wants to continue their group coverage for an available period and accepts the quoted premium. It may be a poor fit when its usual duration would end well before Medicare eligibility; compare another available source of coverage for the remaining time. A Marketplace plan may deserve closer attention when its quoted price is lower, but confirm the enrollment window and provider information before choosing. A different quote or coverage end date could change which option fits.

sections.heading: When Medicare Starts to Matter
sections.body:
Medicare enrollment needs attention before the month you turn 65. Its Initial Enrollment Period begins three months before that month, so add the opening of the period to the coverage timeline you use for early retirement.

Compare the expected end date of your bridge coverage with the Medicare timeline. Do not assume that turning 65, electing COBRA, or keeping another plan answers every enrollment question. Use the [Medicare enrollment periods guide](/guides/medicare-enrollment-periods/) to identify questions to confirm with Medicare.gov about your own dates and coverage.

Medicare costs also belong in a retirement spending estimate after the bridge-coverage period. See the [Medicare costs guide](/guides/medicare-costs-2026-part-b-premium-irmaa/) for the cost topics to investigate. Ask Medicare.gov or a licensed insurance agent to confirm the figures and rules that apply when you enroll.

sections.heading: Early Retirement Health Insurance Checklist Before Leaving Your Job
sections.body:
Get the coverage dates, premiums, and enrollment instructions before you settle on a retirement date. You can put the answers beside your other expense estimates in the [financial independence calculator](/retirement/fire-calculator/). Ask each source for information about the coverage it handles:

- **Your employer:** When would your job-based health coverage end if you retired on the date you are considering? Who administers its continuation coverage?
- **The plan administrator:** Is COBRA available to you and any dependents? What premium would you pay, when would you receive an election notice, and how long could coverage last?
- **HealthCare.gov:** Would the expected loss of your qualifying coverage open a Special Enrollment Period? What Marketplace price appears using your estimated household income?
- **A spouse's plan administrator, if relevant:** Is coverage available to you, what would it cost, and what enrollment date applies?
- **A licensed insurance agent:** Which available plans include the providers you want to check, and which coverage dates still need confirmation?

Keep the answers together. A quoted premium without an enrollment date leaves a gap in your plan, while an enrollment window without a price leaves the retirement budget unfinished. Before setting a departure date, write down your early retirement health insurance choices and confirm their premiums and deadlines with the relevant plan administrators and HealthCare.gov.

This information is for education only and is not individualized insurance, financial, tax, or retirement advice. Confirm decisions for your situation with a licensed insurance agent, certified public accountant, or financial advisor.

faqs.question: How long can you stay on COBRA after retiring?
faqs.answer: COBRA continuation coverage usually lasts up to 18 months. Ask your plan administrator whether it is available to you, when coverage would start, and how long it could last in your situation.

faqs.question: Can you get a Marketplace plan if you retire early?
faqs.answer: You may qualify for a Marketplace Special Enrollment Period if you lose qualifying health coverage. HealthCare.gov lists a window for coverage lost in the past 60 days or expected to end in the next 60 days. Retirement itself is not listed as a qualifying life event, so confirm your enrollment window with HealthCare.gov.

faqs.question: Is COBRA cheaper than a Marketplace plan?
faqs.answer: You need quotes for both to compare them. Under COBRA, you usually pay the full premium, and the charge can be up to 102% of the group plan's cost. Marketplace pricing and possible premium tax credits depend on your estimated household income.

faqs.question: What happens to health insurance at 65?
faqs.answer: Medicare's Initial Enrollment Period begins three months before the month you turn 65. Compare your existing coverage end date with your Medicare enrollment timeline, and confirm the applicable rules with Medicare.gov.

faqs.question: Do you need health insurance if you retire early and are healthy?
faqs.answer: Being healthy does not settle how you would pay for care before Medicare. Compare the coverage and cost of the options available to you, then ask a licensed insurance agent to help confirm any plan details you cannot verify.
